chunks: What is sensor fusion?. The question: What is sensor fusion?
Sensor fusion means combining readings from several sensors to get one estimate that is better than any single sensor could give.
It works because different sensors are bad in different ways. Where one is weak, another is strong, so blending them cancels the weak spots.
Picture walking through a dark room. Counting your steps tells you how far you moved, and it is smooth, but small mistakes pile up the longer you walk.
Now and then you touch a wall, which tells you exactly where you are, but only at that moment. You trust your step count between touches and correct it at each wall.
Sensor fusion does the same, many times a second. One difference: a real filter blends the two all the time instead of only at walls.
The complementary filter is one high-pass and one low-pass that sum to 1.
The gyro owns the high frequencies, the accelerometer owns the low ones; tau sets where the hand-over happens.
Gyroscope: a sensor that measures how fast something is rotating. Adding up its readings over time gives the angle.
Accelerometer: a sensor that measures acceleration, including the pull of gravity, so it can tell which way is down.
Drift: a small steady error that grows as you keep adding readings together. Noise: random jitter on a reading.
Complementary filter: a simple blend that trusts the fast sensor for quick changes and the steady sensor for the long run.
Hold a board perfectly still. The gyroscope should read 0 degrees per second but reads 0. 5. Adding that up gives 30 degrees of false tilt after one minute.
The accelerometer reads the true tilt of 0 degrees, but jitters from sample to sample.
Now, 100 times a second, keep 98 percent of the gyro-updated angle and pull 2 percent toward the accelerometer angle. The false tilt then settles near 0.
25 degrees instead of growing. That is the whole idea.
"Sensor fusion combines several sensors to get an estimate better than any one alone.
They have complementary weaknesses: a gyro is smooth but drifts, an accelerometer is absolute for tilt but noisy.
A complementary filter trusts the gyro in the short term and the accelerometer in the long term, and a Kalman filter does the same optimally by weighting each sensor by its noise variance.
Other examples are GPS plus IMU and camera plus IMU."
